claims.claim: Any consistent formal system F capable of expressing basic arithmetic cannot prove its own consistency using only its own axioms and rules of inference.
claims.plain_english: If a math system works and doesn't contradict itself, it can't prove that it doesn't contradict itself using only its own rules.
claims.evidence_given: Gödel's Second Incompleteness Theorem (1931), established mathematics.
claims.what_would_break_it: A counterexample where a consistent formal system proves its own consistency from within, which would contradict Gödel's proof.

claims.claim: No sufficiently powerful formal language can define its own truth predicate without generating paradox.
claims.plain_english: A system can't define what 'true' means using only its own words without creating a contradiction like 'this sentence is false.'
claims.evidence_given: Tarski's Undefinability Theorem (1936), established mathematical logic.
claims.what_would_break_it: A formal language that defines its own truth predicate without paradox, contradicting Tarski's theorem.

claims.claim: No algorithm can determine, for all possible program-input pairs, whether the program will halt or run forever.
claims.plain_english: A computer can't always predict if another program will stop or keep running forever.
claims.evidence_given: Turing's Halting Problem (1936), established computer science.
claims.what_would_break_it: An algorithm that solves the halting problem for all possible program-input pairs, contradicting Turing's proof.

claims.claim: In any closed system, total entropy can only increase or remain constant over time.
claims.plain_english: In a closed system, disorder always increases or stays the same; things fall apart on their own.
claims.evidence_given: Second Law of Thermodynamics (Clausius/Boltzmann), confirmed by countless physical experiments.
claims.what_would_break_it: A closed system where entropy spontaneously decreases without external input, violating the Second Law.

claims.claim: Erasing one bit of information releases a minimum of kT·ln(2) joules of heat into the environment; information processing has irreducible thermodynamic cost.
claims.plain_english: Thinking and computing always cost energy; there's no free lunch even for information.
claims.evidence_given: Landauer's Principle (1961), supported by thermodynamics and information theory.
claims.what_would_break_it: A process that erases a bit of information without any heat dissipation, violating Landauer's bound.

claims.claim: Any sufficiently complex closed system cannot: prove its own consistency, define its own truth, predict its own behavior, maintain its own order, or process information without irreversible cost.
claims.plain_english: Any complicated system that's closed off can't check itself, define truth for itself, predict itself, keep itself organized, or think without paying a price.
claims.evidence_given: Convergence of the five theorems (Gödel, Tarski, Turing, Second Law, Landauer) across logic, language, computation, physics, and information.
claims.what_would_break_it: A counterexample of a sufficiently complex closed system that succeeds at any of these five tasks, contradicting the unified claim.

claims.claim: The universe has maintained extraordinary order for 13.8 billion years, exhibits truth, maintains consistency, and processes information, despite five proven theorems saying closed systems cannot do these things.
claims.plain_english: The universe stays organized and works consistently, even though math and physics say closed systems can't do that on their own.
claims.evidence_given: Observation of cosmic order, physical laws holding, mathematics working, and information processing (e.g., reading this text).
claims.what_would_break_it: Evidence that the universe is not a closed system, or that the five theorems do not apply to the universe as a whole.

claims.claim: Only a self-grounding terminus—something necessary, self-existent, eternal, and the source of all coherence—can logically explain the persistence of order, truth, consistency, and coherent information in the universe.
claims.plain_english: The only logical explanation for why the universe stays organized and true is something that grounds itself, like God.
claims.evidence_given: Argument from elimination: infinite regress and brute fact are rejected as incoherent or insufficient; the self-grounding terminus is presented as the only remaining option.
claims.what_would_break_it: A coherent alternative explanation that does not rely on a self-grounding entity, or a demonstration that infinite regress or brute fact is logically acceptable.

claims.claim: The required properties of a self-grounding terminus are precisely the classical attributes of God: necessary existence, self-existence (aseity), simplicity, eternality, and the ground of all being.
claims.plain_english: The thing that grounds everything has to have the same qualities that people have traditionally said God has.
claims.evidence_given: Logical deduction from the properties needed for a self-grounding terminus (necessary, self-existent, eternal, simple, ground of being) and their correspondence to classical theism.
claims.what_would_break_it: A demonstration that a self-grounding terminus does not require these specific attributes, or that these attributes are not uniquely associated with God.
